The audit examines the effectiveness of hallucination detection methods for small, quantized on-device large language models (LLMs). It reveals that current evaluation techniques used on larger research models do not translate well to smaller models, resulting in poor ranking transfer and low performance in common detection benchmarks. Additionally, the study highlights methodological weaknesses in existing correctness labels used in evaluations, presenting implications for developers deploying LLMs in resource-constrained environments.

 - Current hallucination detection methods for large language models may not be applicable to smaller models used in practice.
 - The study indicates that performance metrics and detection reliability vary significantly between model types.
 - Methodological flaws in labelers suggest that existing evaluation protocols need to be re-evaluated for accurate assessment.

Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17339

Research indicates that there is an optimal size for large language models (LLMs) in relation to security tasks, as larger models do not always improve performance in these scenarios. The findings suggest that decisions in security based on anomalous inputs may lead to a 'condensing law of security information,' where usable security information can be maximized at a certain model size rather than continuously increasing. Experiments support the concept that security generalization error is U-shaped, implying that there exists a finite model size that minimizes errors associated with security tasks.

 - Usable security information peaks at a specific size, leading to errors at both smaller and larger model sizes.

They have discovered that while this problem is Ackermann-complete for general cases, it can be solved in polynomial time for a specific subset known as alphabetically bidirected VASS. However, the presence of a zero test alters its decidability significantly, complicating the analysis of one-counter automata.

 - Regular separability for bidirected VASS is Ackermann-complete.
 - Alphabetically bidirected VASS allows polynomial-time solutions.
 - Introducing a zero test renders regular separability in one-counter automata undecidable.

Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03313
